Q: SQL query running slow A:

Is this a generated query? About 45% of the code are superfluous brackets, parentheses and redundant code. The illegible where clause boils down to a mere "where the term is either empty or occurs in the first name, the last name or the phone number".

This is necessarily a full table scan. No index can help finding the rows quicker here. But an index covering WHEREand ORDER BY can still help. How is that? The DBMS must read all rows and then check the three columns for a partial match. Then all the found rows must get sorted, and then you'll only take a certain range of those rows. (This paging method using OFFSET is about the slowest possible, by the way.)

If we provide the following index:

CREATE INDEX idx ON candidates (createdon DESC, lastname, availabledate, status, firstname, lastname, phone);

Then the DBMS would find all rows already sorted. Let's say you want the matching rows #5 to #9, then start at the beginning of the index, check every row for a match, skip the first four matches and then take the next 5, and you are done. No additional sorting needed. An index scan is slower than a table scan, but sorting is often a very slow process, so usually we are still better off with the index scan and no additional sort.

Since SQL Server 2008, we can even use a filtered index:

CREATE INDEX idx ON candidates (createdon DESC, lastname, availabledate, firstname, lastname, phone)
WHERE status <> N'System' OR status IS NULL;

What else can we do here? We can pre-compute the numeric phone number by adding a computed column to the table. Then we can access that one instead of the alphanumeric phone number column.

As to the pagination: It is way more performant to remember at what sort key we stopped. Let's take a telephone book. You want to find the first 100 Adams, then the next 100 and so on. At one point you have found the first 10000 and want to look for 10001 to 10100; would you start from the beginning to get there or would you rather remember that the last Adam was Adam Funfrock and continue there?

Your WHERE and ORDER BY clauses would become something like

 WHERE 
 (    c.createdon < @last_createdon
  OR (c.createdon = @last_createdon AND c.lastname > @last_lastname)
  OR (c.createdon = @last_createdon AND c.lastname = @last_lastname AND c.availabledate > @last_availabledate)
  OR (c.createdon = @last_createdon AND c.lastname = @last_lastname AND c.availabledate = @last_availabledate and c.id > @last_id)
 )
 AND (c.Status <> N'System' OR c.Status IS NULL)
 AND
 (
     @__term_0 = N'' 
  OR CHARINDEX(@__term_0, c.FirstName) > 0
  OR CHARINDEX(@__term_0, c.LastName) > 0
  OR CHARINDEX(@__term_0, c.Email) > 0
  OR CHARINDEX(@__term_0, REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(c.Phone, N' ', N''), N'(', N''), N')', N''), N'-', N'')) > 0
  OR CAST(1 AS bit) = CAST(0 AS bit)
 )
 ORDER BY c.createdon DESC, c.lastname, c.availabledate, c.id
 FETCH NEXT @__p_4 ROWS ONLY

Thus you can benefit even more from above index, because the DBMS can get stright to the poition where it was last turn.

Q: Using VBA to save edits to a border in an Inventor 2026 idw file A:

Thanks for the suggestions. There is no error. The code I pasted closes the border without saving the changes. I can remove "On Error Resume Next" and it has no further effect on the outcome

I did find out what the issue was. I was editing the sketch via code using "BorderDefinition.Edit" which from the Autodesk Inventor API Help is as follows
BorderDefinition.Edit( Sketch As DrawingSketch )

I had used "oBorderDef.Edit Nothing" but should have named the sketch created on editing the border as follows.

Dim oEditSketch As DrawingSketch
oBorderDef.Edit oEditSketch

I could then use this in the editing code for example as below
For Each oTextBox In oEditSketch.TextBoxes
